seo.title: Karmic tail 12 13 19 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 13 19 compatibility: The Hanged Man, Death and The Sun in a couple's destiny matrix, read through the Book of Tobit, with a worked example.

title: The 12-13-19 karmic tail in compatibility: The Hanged Man, Death and The Sun
short: The couple's tail 12-13-19 sounds like the opening of a grim fairy tale: first The Hanged Man, then Death, and only at the very end The Sun. There is less to fear in it than it seems. This is the tail of a couple who enter their union with a habit of putting their own lives on hold for other people's peace, who pass through the end of an old form, and who learn the main thing — to live in daylight: to see each other rather than old fears, and to hide neither joy nor trouble.

sections.h2: The 12-13-19 tail as a story: the Book of Tobit
paragraphs: The Book of Tobit is more than two thousand years old. Fragments of it in Aramaic and Hebrew turned up among the Dead Sea Scrolls; Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include it, and the 1611 King James Version printed it among the Apocrypha. It is a family story about two houses in two cities.

In Nineveh lives old Tobit, a righteous man who buries his murdered kinsmen even though he could be killed for it himself. "My neighbours mocked me," he says. One night, back from a burial, he lies down to sleep by the wall of his courtyard, and droppings from the birds fall into his open eyes: "a whiteness came in mine eyes". With him are his wife Anna and his son Tobias. In Ecbatana lives Sara, the only daughter of Raguel. She has been given in marriage seven times, and seven times the bridegroom died on the first night — the story blames the evil spirit Asmodeus. Her father's maids throw it in her face: "thou hast had already seven husbands, neither wast thou named after any of them."

On one and the same day both of them ask God for death: a blind old man in one city and a bride of seven weddings in the other. The story says that both prayers are heard at once and that the answer to both is the same — not death, but a road. Tobit sends his son Tobias to fetch silver once left with a kinsman. A young man who calls himself Azarias is hired as his companion; the reader knows he is the angel Raphael. The road leads across the river Tigris, to Raguel's house where Sara waits, and back again — to a father who cannot see.

Lay the story out chapter by chapter and all three cards of the tail are there, in the same order. Two lives put on hold, and the fear of coming close. A wedding night on which the bride's father digs a grave. A blind man to whom the light comes back. And next to the tail, in the matrix of such couples, stand Judgement, The Lovers or The Devil — and each of these cards has its own scene in the book. The story proves nothing about living people. But as a mirror it is accurate to the smallest detail.

sections.h2: Entry to the task, 12: The Hanged Man — two people who say the same sentence
paragraphs: The entry to the task, point M, is what the couple wants together, its common language. In the couple's reading the same point sits in the sphere "Relationship and common language" and is labelled "Common language". For couples with the 12-13-19 tail, that language is The Hanged Man: a life put on hold for the sake of others.

In the Book of Tobit it can be heard word for word. Sara and Tobias have never seen each other, yet they say one and the same sentence. Sara, who had resolved to end her life, stops herself with the thought of her father: "I am the only daughter of my father… and I shall bring his old age with sorrow unto the grave." Tobias, told about the seven dead bridegrooms, answers the angel: "I am the only son of my father, and I am afraid, lest, if I go in unto her, I die, as the other before" — and so "bring my father's and my mother's life because of me to the grave with sorrow". Later Raguel describes them more precisely than anyone: "two that were the only begotten children of their fathers". Two only children with one and the same fear — of grieving their parents.

There it is, the common language of The Hanged Man: my wish can wait, as long as the people close to me are not hurt. In a living couple it sounds ordinary. "Let's not do it now, Mum is having a hard enough time." The move is put off because Dad won't manage on his own. The wedding is postponed because it would be awkward in front of the family. Each one gives way, and gives way sincerely. Yuliana Lisovskaya describes such couples as a union where one partner is ready to do nothing for themselves and everything for the other, where people take a long time to enter the relationship, and where a decisive step needs a push from outside. In the story the push comes from an angel. In life it comes from a friend who asks "how much longer are you going to wait?", from a job in another city, from a sudden clarity after a long pause.

This language has real strength. The two notice each other's tiredness before a word is said, hear each other out to the end and give way without scenes. They sense each other at a distance: Tobias, the story says, fell in love with Sara before they met, from the angel's words alone — "and his heart was effectually joined to her." The Hanged Man is not just patience: it is the ability to stop and look at life from the other side.

But the entry point stands on the line of tasks, and the wish of the entry easily turns into resistance. Suspension becomes a habit. The two are so busy with other people's peace that their own decision is put off for years. In her prayer Sara asks not for happiness but for quiet: "that I may hear no more the reproach." What matters most becomes what people will say — the maids, the neighbours, the relatives. And the one who keeps giving way starts, one day, to wait in silence for the debt to be repaid.

And there is one detail that holds the whole tail together. By the Tigris, while Tobias is washing, "a fish leaped out of the river, and would have devoured him." The angel does not say "run". He says: "Take the fish," and then: "Open the fish, and take the heart and the liver and the gall, and put them up safely." The fear of the entry is not thrown away: it is hauled onto the bank and kept. The heart and the liver will be needed on the wedding night, the gall at the very end. One fish for three cards. What the two feared at the start later becomes what sets them free and gives them back their sight.

sections.h2: Middle of the task, 13: Death — a grave dug on the wedding night
paragraphs: The middle of the task, point N, is what the couple goes through on the way from the wish of the entry to the main task. Death stands here. In Arthur Edward Waite's old list of divinatory meanings this card has, among other things, the line "for a maid, failure of marriage projects". Sara's seven weddings read like an illustration of it.

The eighth wedding is held that same evening. The bride's father is honest: "I will declare unto thee the truth" — and he tells him about the seven. Tobias lays the heart and liver of the fish on the incense, and the spirit, the story says, flees to Egypt. Then the bridegroom rises and says: "Sister, arise, and let us pray." He asks: "mercifully ordain that we may become aged together." — "And she said with him, Amen."

Then comes the quietest and most frightening scene in the book: "So they slept both that night. And Raguel arose, and went and made a grave, Saying, I fear lest he also be dead." He sends a maid to look and has already decided what will happen: "if he be not, that we may bury him, and no man know it." The maid "found them both asleep". Raguel blesses God and bids "his servants to fill the grave".

The grave is not dug by an enemy. It is dug by a loving father whom the past has taught to expect the end. In the middle of this tail it is not the union that dies but the expectation that it will end like the ones before. Among the difficulties of Death in a couple Lisovskaya names carrying the traits of former partners over onto the present one. In the story the bride's father does it; in life anyone can — relatives, friends, the partners themselves. The suitcase that, after the last break-up, was never quite unpacked. Mum's "let's see how long this one lasts". The habit of checking whether the other will leave or not. The attempt to brace in advance for the blow so that it will hurt less later. Nothing wicked — only fear, digging a pit at night while the two of them sleep.

The second half of Death is leaving. Raguel holds his son-in-law for a fourteen-day feast and binds him by an oath that "he should not depart". Tobias asks: "Let me go, for my father and my mother look no more to see me." Letting them go, Raguel hands over half his goods and tells his daughter: "Honour thy father and thy mother in law, which are now thy parents." Benebell Wen writes that "traditionally, Key 13 is related to death and birth, property and inheritance, society and family". The middle of the tail runs through exactly these places: home, inheritance, parents. What dies is the role of the "only begotten children". The two stop being first of all somebody's son and daughter and become a couple.

Meanwhile, in Nineveh, a mother is mourning a living son. "My son is dead," says Anna, and she "went out every day into the way which they went". Two families in two cities are ready to bury a man who is alive and married. This is how the middle of this tail looks from outside: to the people close by it seems that something is dying — and that is true, the old order is dying. Waite distinguished natural death from "mystical death", which he called "a change in the form of consciousness" while still in this life. For a couple it is a change in the form of the union: who belongs to whom, whose home comes first, with whom the holidays are spent.

In the positive, Lisovskaya sees in a couple's Death living proof that life goes on after hard times: the two accept each other's past and move on, and take changes in each other easily. In the negative, there are so many changes that the other has nothing left to lean on, or one partner hurries the other to change before they are ready. The middle of this tail asks not for speed but for an honest farewell to the old.

sections.h2: Main task, 19: The Sun — the whiteness, the kid and the secret of a king
paragraphs: The main task, point D, is read by Lisovskaya mainly through its negative: what does not work for the couple and what it has to learn. The Sun stands here. In the Book of Tobit its negative is shown not on the young couple but on the older one — on Tobit and Anna.

When the kinsman who has been feeding the blind Tobit goes away, Anna keeps the house: she takes in women's work, spinning wool for the rich. One day her employers give her a kid on top of her wages. The kid bleats, and her husband asks: "From whence is this kid? is it not stolen?" Anna answers: "It was given for a gift more than the wages." "Howbeit I did not believe her," Tobit admits, and orders her to give it back. Then Anna says the words after which he prays for death: "Where are thine alms and thy righteous deeds? behold, thou and all thy works are known." Rembrandt painted this quarrel in 1626, at the age of twenty; "Tobit and Anna with the Kid" is in the Rijksmuseum.

This is The Sun in the negative: one partner does not see the light the other has brought into the house. The partner's success is met with an interrogation, righteousness turns into suspicion, suspicion into a barbed reply. Among the tasks of The Sun Lisovskaya names both harsh criticism and the failure to let the partner's victory be the partner's own. In the story all of it fits into one scene with a kid. Either of the two can be the suspicious one: gender decides nothing here. In a living couple the kid is the bonus one of them mentions over dinner while the other asks: "For what, exactly?" The present from colleagues met with a jealous "why all of a sudden?" The praise nobody repeats in front of the family so as not to look boastful.

Anna has a second line too, spoken on the day her son sets off: "Be not greedy to add money to money: but let it be as refuse in respect of our child." She calls her son "the staff of our hand". One scene holds both edges of The Sun's negative: the pursuit of money and position at the family's expense — and an attachment to a loved one so strong that they are not allowed to leave for a life of their own.

The Sun comes back bitter. The angel tells Tobias to anoint his father's eyes with the fish's gall. "And when his eyes began to smart, he rubbed them; And the whiteness pilled away from the corners of his eyes." The first thing the man who can see again says is: "behold, I see my son Tobias." Not "I see the light" — "I see my son". That is the main task of a couple with the 12-13-19 tail: to see the person, not one's own fear about them. And it stings. The truth that removes the whiteness burns at first, like gall.

Then Tobit walks to the gate of Nineveh to meet his daughter-in-law — in front of everyone, "rejoicing", and "they which saw him go marvelled, because he had received his sight." The Sun is not hidden. In the positive, Lisovskaya's Sun is a couple whose house is warm and full of people, where each succeeds in their own work and pulls the other up, and where their well-being shows from outside. Waite's old divinatory vocabulary raises a smile here: for Death it has "failure of marriage projects", for The Sun "fortunate marriage". These are words from a list of fortune-telling meanings, not a promise. But this couple's road runs exactly between two lines of the same vocabulary.

At the end the companion gives his name — "I am Raphael" — and leaves the family a rule that sounds like a formula for the main task: "It is good to keep close the secret of a king, but it is honourable to reveal the works of God." And a last instruction: "write all things which are done in a book." In this story everything began in secret: burials after sundown, a companion's borrowed name, a grave that "no man know it". Everything ends told in daylight. Other people's secrets the couple keeps. Its own — joy, gratitude, the good things that have happened to the two of them — it says out loud.

sections.h2: What the numbers record: a tail that is born only between two people
paragraphs: The 12-13-19 tail occurs in roughly one couple in 57 (1.739%) — 19th place among the 97 couple tails. Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. And here the numbers reveal something that a single card cannot show.

**The Hanged Man of the entry is shared.** The tail is made from only three combinations of personal tails: 18-9-9 and 21-4-10 (88% of such couples), 18-6-6 and 21-7-13 (11%), 18-3-12 and 21-10-7 (2%). One partner's personal tail always begins with The Moon, the other's with The World: 18 + 21 = 39 → 3 + 9 = 12. The suspension at the entry is a joint invention, not a trait of one person: in 88% of such couples neither of the two personal tails contains 12, 13 or 19. The Sun is in none of the six personal tails: this couple's main task is born only from the sum.

**The middle breaks the rule of a single person.** In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is the entry plus the main task. If the couple were one person, it would come out as 12 + 19 = 31 → 4, The Emperor. But the couple's middle is added up from the partners' middles: 9 + 4, 6 + 7 or 3 + 10 — and the result is 13. That is why 12-13-19 is impossible as a personal tail. Everything else in this triple is built "as in one person": the couple's entry, just as in a personal matrix, equals the main task plus the centre, 19 + 20 = 39 → 12. Only the middle breaks. And it breaks in a curious way: 1 + 3 = 4. Where one person would hold the form, like The Emperor, two people get the same four, but unreduced — as Death, which changes the form. This is our reading of the arithmetic, not a rule of the method.

**The centre of every such couple is 20, Judgement.** The centre of a couple's matrix is the atmosphere inside the union, what is not on show. For Lisovskaya, Judgement in a couple is above all kin and family: the parents' voice sounds in the couple's home even when they are not around. The whole Book of Tobit stands on this: the marriage is made "after the law of Moses", because "thou art her cousin, and she is thine", the bride's father himself writes "an instrument of covenants, and sealed it", and Sara's "right of inheritance doth rather appertain to thee than to any other." In the positive, Judgement in the centre gives a couple whom the relatives accept, where mistakes are forgiven and the two support each other even when one of them is wrong. In the negative, a union held together by the elders' approval, and a partner who decides nothing without their parents. For a couple whose common language is the fear of grieving father and mother, this is the main place where the Hanged Man of the entry can get stuck.

**The couple's values are The Lovers or The Devil.** "The couple's values", the spiritual purpose, are 6, The Lovers, in 77.3% of such couples and 15, The Devil, in 22.7%. Both cards are present on Tobias's wedding night. His prayer begins with the first human couple: "Thou madest Adam, and gavest him Eve his wife for an helper and stay". He says: "I take not this my sister for lust, but uprightly" — the choice of The Lovers, made consciously and out loud. And the Devil of this book is Asmodeus, of whom Tobias says: "a wicked spirit loveth her, which hurteth no body, but those which come unto her". A love that kills anyone who comes near the beloved is an exact image of The Devil in a couple: attachment that has turned into ownership. Lisovskaya's final thought about the fifteenth energy: nobody belongs to anybody.

Two people were born on 14.09.1975 and 14.10.1975. The first one's personal tail is 18-9-9, the second one's is 21-4-10: the most common combination for 12-13-19. The points of the couple's tail add up like this:

The couple's centre is 9 + 11 = 20, Judgement, as in every couple with this tail. The values of these two are 15, The Devil: they belong to the smaller group. If the middle were counted by the personal formula, it would come out as 12 + 19 = 31 → 4, but the couple has its own — the sum of the personal middles, 9 + 4. And The Sun also appears for this couple in the sphere "Why you met", at the point "What to create together": the sum of the birth months, 9 + 10 = 19.

sections.h2: Waite and Wen: one white horse for Death and The Sun
paragraphs: This section is about the Waite–Smith deck and the texts of Waite and Wen; the cards on this site are drawn in their own way. In the books themselves the three cards of the tail hold on to one another.

Waite ends his description of The Hanged Man with a sentence that already contains the next two cards: "He who can understand that the story of his higher nature is imbedded in this symbolism will receive intimations concerning a great awakening that is possible, and will know that after the sacred Mystery of Death there is a glorious Mystery of Resurrection." Suspension, then Death, then light — the order of the 12-13-19 tail is written by Waite into one sentence about the twelfth card.

Death and The Sun are linked by a horse. Wen describes the rider of the thirteenth card as "an armored skeleton" who "waves a black flag bearing the Rosicrucian Rose" and "rides a white steed". The child of the nineteenth card, in her own words, is also "riding a white steed, waving a red banner"; in Waite he is "mounted on a white horse". The horse is the same. What changes is the rider — the skeleton becomes a child — and the colour of the banner. For a couple it is an exact image: the road and the union stay the same; what changes is who holds the reins — fear or simplicity. The sun that on Death still stands on the horizon rises overhead on the nineteenth card.

And in older decks, Waite writes, The Sun was a card of two: it showed "a wall suggesting an enclosure—as it might be, a walled garden—wherein are two children, either naked or lightly clothed, facing a water, and gambolling, or running hand in hand." In the old picture the couple's main task is two people in one light.

There are clues too in the cards that stand beside the tail. On Judgement, the centre of all such couples, "the dead are rising from their tombs—a woman on the right, a man on the left hand, and between them their child" — like the family in Nineveh, where the son had already been mourned. The summons from above, Waite says, "is heard and answered from within." Waite describes The Lovers "as if Adam and Eve when they first occupied the paradise of the earthly body", and The Devil with the same two, but now "as if Adam and Eve after the Fall", in chains. The values of couples with this tail are one and the same first human couple: free in 77% and chained in 23%.

sections.h2: How a couple with the 12-13-19 tail changes the script
paragraphs: The tail neither condemns nor promises. It shows where the couple's familiar circle lies and where the way out of it is. In the story the miracles are the angel's work, but every step is taken by people: they take the fish, rise and pray together, fill the grave, leave the father-in-law's house, anoint a father's eyes, walk out to the gate.

ul: **Name the shared fear.** Say out loud that both are afraid of grieving their parents, and agree whose grief the couple is ready to carry and whose it is not. Suspension lives on silence.

**Keep the fish.** The fear of the beginning is no reason to run and no reason to stay silent. Take it apart together: what exactly each one fears. Then it becomes knowledge about each other rather than a wall.
**Fill the grave.** Do not measure the partner by past stories — one's own or other people's. Finish unpacking the "spare suitcase" and stop checking whether this one will leave too.
**Leave the parents without leaving them.** A home of one's own, holidays of one's own, an order of one's own — and gratitude to the elders without reporting to them.
**Don't ask where the kid came from.** Accept the partner's success, gift and praise without an interrogation, and be glad for them in front of other people.

**Keep what is others', reveal what is one's own.** Guard other people's secrets, but speak to each other directly about one's own joy and one's own trouble before they turn into whiteness over the eyes.

**Entry to the task — 12, The Hanged Man.** The couple's common language: to wait, to give way, to sacrifice themselves so that the people close to them are not hurt. Hence tact and tenderness — and a long suspension, when two people take years to make their own move.

**Middle of the task — 13, Death.** The road runs through an ending. What dies is not the union but an old form: the role of obedient children, earlier stories, the expectation that this union will end the way the previous ones did.
**Main task — 19, The Sun.** To learn to see the partner as they are, to be glad of their success without suspicion, to say difficult things out loud and not to hide happiness.

intro: None of the three cards predicts events: Death in the middle is not a break-up, and The Sun at the end is not a promise. This is a picture of how a couple lives through its task. And the picture has a very old double — a story in which the three cards come in exactly this order.

faq.q: What does the 12-13-19 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail where the entry to the task is 12, The Hanged Man, the middle is 13, Death, and the main task is 19, The Sun. The two enter the union with a common language of sacrifice and waiting, pass through the end of an old form — the roles of "obedient children", earlier stories and fears — and learn to live in daylight: to see each other without suspicion, to talk about difficult things and not to hide joy.

faq.q: Does Death in the middle of a couple's tail mean a break-up?
faq.a: No. The numbers of the matrix do not predict events. Death in the middle of the tail means that the couple's road runs through the end of an old order: old expectations, familiar roles, life under the parents' roof. In the Book of Tobit a grave is dug on the wedding night, but by morning it is filled in: what dies is not the union but the fear that it will end.

faq.q: Why does a couple have the 12-13-19 tail when the partners' personal tails usually lack these numbers?
faq.a: The couple's points are added up from the matching points of two personal matrices. The entry 12 always comes from one partner's Moon and the other's World (18 + 21 = 39 → 12), the middle 13 from the personal middles, the main task 19 from the personal main tasks. In 88% of such couples neither personal tail contains 12, 13 or 19, and nobody has The Sun: this task is born only between two people.

faq.q: Why is the middle of the tail 13 and not 12 + 19?
faq.a: The middle of a couple's tail is not recalculated from the two outer numbers; it is added up from the partners' middles. By the personal formula it would come out as 12 + 19 = 31 → 4, The Emperor. That is why 12-13-19 never occurs as a personal tail: this order exists only in a couple's matrix.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. The Hanged Man, Death and The Sun form a couple's tail only in the order 12-13-19: entry to the task 12, middle 13, main task 19. No other arrangement of these three numbers appears among the 97 couple tails.

report: On the wedding night the bride's father got up, went out and dug the bridegroom a grave. "I fear lest he also be dead," he said. His daughter's seven earlier weddings had ended with the bridegroom's death; this was the eighth. The maid sent to look found the young couple asleep, and by morning the grave had been filled. This scene from the Book of Tobit is the key to the couple's tail 12-13-19. The Hanged Man, Death and The Sun come in the ancient story in the same order, and what dies in it is not the union but the expectation that it will end like the ones before.

report: The Sun comes back bitter. The father's eyes are anointed with the fish's gall: "And when his eyes began to smart, he rubbed them; And the whiteness pilled away from the corners of his eyes."
